summary: Explains why the DNS Server and Resolver MIB extensions were never deployed after six years as proposed standards, and recommends retiring them by moving them to Historical status.

plainLanguage.summary: It explains why a tool for watching the phone book was never used and suggests retiring it.

subtitle: Why DNS management tools were never actually used.

tldr.problem: RFC 1611 and 1612 define DNS Server and Resolver MIB extensions for SNMP management, but after more than six years as Proposed Standards, they were never deployed in the real world.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC examines why the MIB extensions failed: poor initial goals, too much complexity, a focus on one implementation, disagreement about scope, and an unrealistic development timeline.
tldr.outcome: The author recommends moving the DNS MIB extensions to Historic status and offers lessons learned for future MIB development.

today: RFC 1611 and 1612 are now Historic. This RFC, 3197, documents the lessons learned from this effort.

sections.title: A Management Tool That Never Shipped
sections.content:
During the 1990s, MIB (Management Information Base) extensions were being written for every protocol. The DNS working group created MIB extensions for DNS servers and resolvers, expecting network administrators would use SNMP to monitor and manage DNS systems.

After more than six years of development and standardization work, these MIB extensions were never actually deployed or implemented. They remain as Proposed Standards with no real-world use.
sections.plainLanguage: Engineers designed a tool to watch and control DNS servers using the standard network management system. But by the time they finished, nobody wanted to use it.

sections.title: Why the MIB Extensions Failed
sections.content:
The DNS MIB extensions ran into multiple fundamental problems. First, the working group lacked clear agreement on what should be included, just that something should exist. As development continued, the specification grew too large, often mirroring the statistics kept by the BIND implementation rather than being truly implementation-neutral.

The SNMP framework itself proved inadequate for the task. Complex indexing requirements for the resolver cache exceeded known length limits in some SNMP implementations. The dominant DNS implementation, BIND, had no way to actually implement these MIB extensions without a subagent protocol like AgentX, which did not exist yet.

By the time AgentX became viable, interest in the project had evaporated. The working group had tired of the effort, the document had become too large and unwieldy, and clear consensus on the approach never materialized.
sections.plainLanguage: The tool was too big, it was built for one particular DNS program instead of all of them, and SNMP was not really the right way to do this kind of management.

sections.title: Lessons and Retirement
sections.content:
The author recommends reclassifying RFC 1611 and 1612 as Historic documents. The experience teaches important lessons: define clear goals first, keep specifications small and focused, do not add variables just because someone thinks they would be useful to measure, and recognize when a tool like SNMP is not the right fit for the task at hand.

This RFC documents those lessons so that future standards efforts can learn from this experience.
sections.plainLanguage: When you plan a standards project, start with a clear goal, keep it simple, and pick the right tool. This project failed because it did none of those things.
